I'm a campaign manager at SAFE, and on behalf of the Commissioner for Animals
Alliance, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today.
I'll get right into it. This petition calls on Parliament to
create an independent commissioner for animals to provide impartial
oversight and accountability of our animal welfare system.
At its core, this is about a simple principle, that laws and
systems intended to protect vulnerable groups should have
non-partisan oversight. This principle is recognized in many other
areas. For example, we have independent commissioners and officers of
Parliament to help protect the interests of children, the environment,
human rights, our aged community, and privacy.
However, animals, despite being recognized as sentient beings and
protected under law, do not have impartial non-partisan
representation.
Let's look at the problem we're trying to solve.
The Animal Welfare Act is generally regarded as a strong piece of legislation,
and the issue here isn't that we lack animal welfare laws.
The issue is that without non-biased, independent oversight, our animal
welfare system is failing the animals it was designed to protect.
The Animal Welfare Act itself is now 25 years old, and
many of the other laws and frameworks that affect animals are older
still.
Much of our animal welfare regulatory system is no longer fit for purpose,
and independent oversight of that system is urgently needed to
improve transparency, accountability, and effectiveness.
Currently, responsibility for animal welfare sits within structures
that also hold responsibility for growing agricultural productivity,
increasing exports, and supporting industry that profit from the use of
animals. This results in real or perceived conflicts of
interest and leads to animal welfare considerations frequently falling
secondary to industry and economic objectives.
This doesn't mean the people working within the system are failing.
Rather, it means the system itself lacks an independent mechanism
capable of ensuring animal welfare outcomes are genuinely
prioritized.
So why is an independent commissioner needed?
The remit of a commissioner would not replace existing agencies or advisory
committees.
Rather, it would address what is currently missing, and that is independent
scrutiny.
MPI has, through its own admission to this committee, identified that
concerns about the agency's dual responsibility have existed for
many years.
A report released by the New Zealand Animal Law Association in
December last year highlighted the pressing need for independent
oversight of animal welfare and identified several issues with the
current system, including conflicts of interest, lack of independent
oversight, poor enforcement of legislation, and insufficient
resourcing.
The findings of NZALA's report
present a clear case for establishing an independent commissioner
to provide oversight of this framework and enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act.
SPCA has submitted that this is an opportunity to recommend targeted
and proportionate reform that will both strengthen our animal welfare system
and help ensure it meets statutory obligations and public
expectations.
It's also worth noting the support that is emerging across the political spectrum.
The Green Party has long supported the establishment of an independent
commissioner. National MP Barbara Kuriger has attended our last few
parliamentary events and been supportive of the concept, and discussions with Labor
indicate that their main concern appears to be cost rather than the concept itself.
I'd now like to turn to the importance of public confidence.
When decision-making processes are perceived as being influenced by industries,
organizations, or individuals with direct economic interest in the
outcome, public trust can be significantly undermined.
New Zealanders have high expectations of how animals are treated, and polling
undertaken last year by SAFE and Verian confirmed that people certainly
expect more than what the current system is delivering.
This polling told us that 96% of Kiwis believe it's
important to protect animals from cruelty and neglect.
In addition to that
Decisions relating to animal welfare law are made by an
independent and impartial party, and 67% support
the idea of New Zealand having a commissioner to oversee animal
welfare.
An independent commissioner would certainly help strengthen public confidence that
decisions are being made transparently and with the welfare of animals as a
priority, rather than being shaped by industry objectives or vested
interests.
To briefly address the topic of budget,
I recognize that any proposal for a new public office needs to be considered
alongside competing funding priorities and the responsible use of
public resources.
Through the identification of synergies and systemic improvements, a
commissioner for animals will improve overall efficiencies in New Zealand's
approach to the oversight of animal welfare and enforcement of our
legislation now and into the future.
Establishing a commissioner to improve our nation's approach to
animal welfare will not only uphold the value we place on the health and
well-being of animals, but it will also help protect our international
and trade reputations. We do not believe this to be a question of can New
Zealand afford to do this? Rather, that we can't afford not to.
I'll speak briefly now about what I'd like to think of as constructive
reform. Unfortunately, this is not a radical
proposal. It is proportionate and supported not only by the
SPCA and NZALA, but also by the Commissioner for Animals
Alliance, a strong and diverse coalition of 22 animal
protection organizations united behind this call for reform.
This follows a model already familiar within our constitutional framework, with
Parliament recognizing issues that are important enough to warrant an independent
oversight body. A few examples being the
Commissioner for the Environment, who provides independent scrutiny of
environmental issues, the Children's Commissioner, who provides independent
oversight of matters relating to children, and the Privacy Commissioner, who
provides independent oversight, monitoring, and reporting on matters affecting
privacy.
This proposal applies the same governance principle, that
our animal welfare system depends on the strength and integrity of the
framework supporting it. Ultimately, this is
about ensuring the system functions as intended
and that the welfare of animals is genuinely prioritized.
Finally, I'd like to outline why we believe a Commissioner
for Animals would benefit New Zealand and why Parliament should support this
petition.
The request in this petition is measured and reasonable.
We're not asking Parliament to resolve every animal issue right now.
We're asking Parliament to acknowledge that a system responsible for protecting
hundreds of millions of sentient beings should have independent
oversight and accountability.
And the establishment of a Commissioner for Animals would help ensure better
transparency and accountability, adequate consideration of scientific
evidence, it would bolster public confidence, and it would ensure a more
consistent application of animal welfare legislation.
These are all goals that are not only in the best interests of animals, they're
also in the best interest of regulators, policymakers, industry,
and the public. We need independent oversight and
accountability to support a system we can all rely on and be proud of.
In closing, our animal welfare system is fundamentally broken, and this
allows for animals to be the victims of severe cruelty, exploitation,
and neglect. The 22 member organizations of the Commissioner for Animals
Alliance emphasize the urgent need for improvement to ensure all
practices and policies for the care and welfare of animals is developed without
bias and are consistent with the intentions of our animal welfare
legislation. This is a unique opportunity that would bring New
Zealand into line with other countries making significant progress
in strengthening animal welfare protections and oversight.
A Commissioner for Animals offers a practical, balanced, and constructive step
forward, supporting the government's commitment to animal welfare and
resulting in significantly improved outcomes for animals.
I respectfully request the Petitions Committee recommends that the House
considers establishing a Commission for Animals as an important step in
improving New Zealand's animal welfare system.

New Zealand has a strong and internationally respected
animal welfare regulatory system.

One of the strengths of New Zealand's animal welfare system is that

institutions.
Parliament sets the legislative framework.
Ministers are accountable for decisions.
Independent advisory committees provide expert advice.
MPI and SPCA undertake compliance and enforcement

Public consultation also gives New Zealanders a direct voice in

Together, these different roles create multiple checks,

challenge. Independent advice is a
cornerstone of the system. The National Animal Welfare

The review concluded that the system has served New Zealand well, is

The review also identified opportunities for continuous
improvement in areas such as governance, stakeholder

processes.
MPI has accepted the review's recommendations.
We have an implementation program of work underway and
is using the recommendations to further strengthen an already sound
and effective system.
Overall, MPI is confident that New Zealand has a strong animal
welfare regulatory system that combines independent advice,
robust enforcement, public accountability, and a
commitment to continuous improvement. Thank you.
